label: Hell and Judgment
framing: Hell is the hardest doctrine the church holds, and it should never be held lightly or with relish. Scripture presents it not as God's eagerness to punish but as the terrible ratification of a person's refusal of him, the door, as one writer put it, locked from the inside.
cultural: Our age finds the very idea offensive, and the church has too often deserved the offense, wielding hell as a threat and a recruiting tool. Yet the same culture that recoils at judgment longs for justice and rages when the wicked go free. Scripture holds both, that God will not let evil have the last word and that he takes no pleasure in the death of anyone.
historical: The church has never spoken with one voice here. Augustine in the fifth century held the traditional view of eternal conscious punishment, while figures from Origen in the third century to some modern evangelicals have argued for conditional immortality or a wider hope. C.S. Lewis in 1945 portrayed hell as the self curved finally inward, a place its residents prefer to surrender. The creeds affirm that Christ will come to judge, and leave the rest to him.
application: Hold this doctrine with tears, never satisfaction, remembering you were not spared because you deserved it. Let it sober your witness without weaponizing it, since fear is a poor evangelist and love a better one. And let the reality of judgment drive you not to threaten your neighbor but to long for his rescue, and to leave the verdict to the Judge who is also the one who died for him.

verses.text: Far be it from You to do such a thing—to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked are treated alike. Far be it from You! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?”
verses.where: As the LORD's visitors set out toward Sodom, Abraham pleads for the city and presses the question that grounds all his pleading: will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right? The site's plain note says God did not rebuke the question but let Abraham press it again and again, and that people of faith may bring their hardest questions about God's justice to God himself.

verses.text: Say to them: ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live. Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?’
verses.where: To exiles crushed by their guilt, God swears by his own life that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and calls them to turn and live. The site's note says the passage's main claim is that God is not keeping a ledger to trap anyone; he is calling everyone to turn and live.

verses.text: The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
verses.where: Against scoffers who say Christ's coming will never arrive, Peter says the Lord is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. The delay that looks like absence is mercy. The site's plain note asks whether you have mistaken God's patience for slowness, and whom you know who needs time to turn.

verses.text: For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him. Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.
verses.where: The Son was not sent to condemn the world but to save it. The site's note says judgment follows in the Gospel as the consequence of rejecting the rescue, not as the reason for the mission, and its plain note says these serious words are not meant to frighten anyone into faith but to show how much is offered.

verses.text: And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
verses.where: Jesus' last great discourse in Matthew ends with two outcomes side by side, eternal punishment and eternal life. The site's note says faithful Christians differ on whether eternal here requires unending conscious experience, final destruction, or an age-long punishment that ends, and that the verse leaves no doubt the outcome is final. It also says the last word of the discourse is life.

verses.text: “Lord,” someone asked Him, “will only a few people be saved?” Jesus answered, “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
verses.where: Someone asks Jesus whether only a few will be saved, and he answers with a command instead of a number: make every effort to enter through the narrow door. The site's note says the question treats salvation as a statistic to be known and Jesus treats it as a door to be entered. Its plain note says the passage is not meant to scare anyone into sleepless fear: the door is there, and it is open.

verses.text: And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And there were open books, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books.
verses.where: John sees the dead, great and small, standing before the throne and judged by what they have done, with the Book of Life open beside the other books. The site's plain note says the church confesses this judgment, that the notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person because that belongs to God alone, and that the judge is the Jesus who died for sinners.

verses.text: In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him. There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love.
verses.where: John says that love perfected among believers gives them confidence on the day of judgment, because perfect love drives out fear. The site's note says that for those who have come to know God's love, judgment is no longer a thing to dread, because that love rests on what God has done, not on how well we have loved.

verses.text: God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand. He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.
verses.where: Paul says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate his righteousness, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus. The site's note calls the cross the place where God's justice and mercy meet, and says Christians describe how in different ways. God does not stand outside judgment; in Christ he bears its cost himself.

misread.taken: The story of the rich man and Lazarus is read as a literal map of the world after death, the flames, the drop of water, the conversation across a chasm, and used to describe in detail what the lost are suffering now.
misread.says: The site's plain note says most read it as a parable: it begins like the parables around it and uses pictures, a finger, a tongue, a chasm, that are hard to take as a plain map of the unseen world. Its note on verse 26 says the point of the chasm is finality: death fixes the outcome of a life. And the rich man's sin was not his wealth. Lazarus lay at his gate, the rich man knew his name, and he never once fed him; the story asks who lies at yours.
misread.text: But Abraham answered, ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony. And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’

whole: If fear of hell is keeping you awake, or you are grieving someone who died without clear faith, or thoughts of judgment have come with thoughts of hurting yourself, tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. People come to this question from very different places. Some were frightened as children by preaching that seemed to enjoy the fire. Some lie awake afraid they are not really saved. Some are grieving a father or a friend and cannot stop wondering where they are now. And some cannot see how a good God could judge anyone at all, and suspect the doctrine says more about the people who preach it than about God.

Scripture speaks of judgment soberly and never with relish. The creeds confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and Jesus himself warned of a real and final judgment, many of his sternest warnings aimed at the religious. The same Bible says the Judge of all the earth will do what is right, that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, that he is patient and does not want anyone to perish, and that the Son came not to condemn the world but to save it. Judgment is not the opposite of God's love. The site's note on 1 John 4 says love that did not oppose what destroys the beloved would be indifference, not love, and that the cross shows both at once: God does not overlook sin, and he bears its cost himself.

So the wisdom here begins with the question Jesus turned around. When someone asked whether only a few would be saved, he answered with an invitation to come in, not a number. Hold the warnings as warnings to yourself before anyone else. The site's notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person, because that belongs to God alone. If you are grieving someone who died without clear faith, the note on Revelation 20 says the passage does not tell us what passed between that person and God at the end, but it does tell us who the judge is: the Jesus who died and rose again. And if you are afraid for yourself, hear the one who warns as the same one who says come to me; perfect love drives out fear because it rests on what God has done.

The hope here is the character of the Judge. Abraham trusted that God's justice would be better than his own, not worse. John says those who know God's love can have confidence on the day of judgment. The judge is the Lamb who was slain, and the last word of Jesus' great warning in Matthew is life. Whatever Christians conclude on the questions they still debate, none of it is a reason to hurry anyone into fear, and all of it is a reason to come home.

differ.share: The creeds confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and Christians agree that Jesus warned of a real and final judgment, that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and that no one but God knows the eternal state of any particular person. They differ on what that judgment is like and whether it lasts forever.

views.name: Endless, conscious separation from God
views.body: The view most widely held through church history is that the punishment of the lost is endless, conscious separation from God. Its defenders point to Matthew 25:46, where the same word, eternal, is used for the punishment and for the life, and Augustine argued that if one is endless the other must be too.

views.name: Eternal in its result
views.body: Others hold that the finally impenitent will at last cease to exist, so that the punishment is eternal in its result, not as endless suffering. They point to Jesus' warning of the one who can destroy both soul and body, and to the wages of sin being death.

views.name: A hope of final restoration
views.body: A minority hope that God's love will in the end restore all people. It has appeared in church history, but the church has generally not affirmed universal salvation, and the New Testament's warnings are severe and real.

differ.after: The site's notes on Matthew 25 and Revelation 20 and its Honest Answer on hell set out these views and do not settle the question. Each tries to keep both God's justice and his love, and each has texts it struggles with. None of them tells anyone who will be there.

deep.sit: Is your fear of judgment pointed at yourself, at someone you love, or at God, and what would it change to look first at who the Judge is?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note asks whether you think of God's judgment as good news or bad news, and invites you to see it from the side of the poor and the wronged, for whom a fair judge is the best news there is.
prayer.text: Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it. Let the fields exult, and all that is in them. Then all the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the LORD, for He is coming— He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness.

careLines.text: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has.
Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust.
If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
